newsitem.title: FRANCE: Hip French radio NRJ puts case in newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Hip French radio NRJ puts case in newspapers.

text.p: French radio station NRJ, one of the country's hippest music stations, took a battle for the radio waves to the pages of the nation's most staid newspapers on Tuesday with full-page advertisements in Le Figaro and Le Monde.
"Halte a l'intox!" (Stop the bullshit), the ad, aimed at those newspapers' readership of members of Parliament and other decision-makers, read in huge black capital letters.
The message was timed to coincide with first reading of a broadcasting bill in the National Assembly lower house on Tuesday that contains provisions NRJ says could threaten its development.
NRJ said publishing group Hachette and Luxembourg's CLT, owners of mainstream stations Europe 1 and RTL respectively, had been lobbying to get priority in the assigning of FM frequencies.
The broadcasting bill would give broadcasting watchdog Conseil Superieur de l'Audiovisuel (CSA) a remit to review the use of the FM band in France.
If NRJ's rivals do get priority for FM frequencies, NRJ would be marginalised, said Marc Pallain, a director of NRJ.
"That would block us totally, it would seriously hold back our development," Pallain told Reuters.
He said NRJ was the only independent competitor to the two radio giants, which he said were trying to recoup their lag among younger listeners by launching their own music stations.
Europe 1 has launched Europe 2 and RFM, while RTL has created RTL2 and Fun Radio.
NRJ, which also runs Cherie FM, has the beginnings of a third station called Rires et Chansons, which currently operates in Paris, Lyon and a handful of other towns, Pallain said.
If NRJ is sent to the back of the queue for FM frequencies, Rires et Chansons will be nipped in the bud, he said.

RTL, Europe 1 and RMC, the three general privately-owned radio stations, simply want to be carried on FM frequencies all over France, Stephane Duhamel, deputy programmes director at RTL, told Reuters.
He said NRJ currently had a wider national coverage on FM than the general stations, excluding their music station subsidiaries.
"RTL does not cover a series of major towns, from Dunkirk to Perpignan, from Calais to Menton, on FM," Duhamel said.
Public station France Inter is the only general radio station to have complete national coverage on FM, he said.
No one was immediately available to comment at Europe 1.
NRJ's advert cited CSA figures showing that Europe 1 reached a total of 51 million people, of whom 35.6 million on FM, while RTL reached 49 million, of whom 36 million on FM.
NRJ itself reaches 39 million people, it said, but gave no breakdown between FM and AM.
